newsitem.title: USA: World Bank delays Croatia loan debate at US request.
newsitem.headline: World Bank delays Croatia loan debate at US request.

text.p: The World Bank, bowing to a request from the United States, has postponed debate on a $30 million loan to help Croatian banks.
A World Bank press officer said the discussions, initially due on Tuesday, had been postponed at the request of the international organisation's U.S. executive director.
"It may be taken up at the next board meeting, but we do not have a date yet," she said.

A U.S. official said on Monday that Washington was asking the World Bank to postpone the release of the loan because Zagreb had not followed through on commitments on extraditing suspected war criminals made under the Dayton peace accord.
"We intend to send concrete signals on a weekly and monthly basis," the official said.
"Right now, in our view, they need to receive a signal that they haven't continued the path toward progress," he added, referring to pledges on suspected war criminals.
At the State Department, spokesman John Dinger said the current delay was for two days, but the United States hoped for a longer postponement and was seeking support for this from U.S. allies.

Dinger said Washington wants the loan debate delayed while it monitors progress in three areas of concern -- Croatia's use of its influence in bringing war criminals to justice, the need for concrete progress on the return of Serb refugees and other displaced persons and the need for more border crossings with Bosnia.

"We believe that Croatia's lack of cooperation on Dayton (peace accords) undermines prospects for regional stability and also calls into question Croatia's commitment to implement and sustain economic programmes that are necessary for prosperity," Dinger said.

Croatia extradited its first war crimes suspect to the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague in April, days after the West tightened pressure on Zagreb. But the U.S. official said there had been no real movement since then.

The U.S. made its position clear after several influential Democratic and Republican senators wrote to Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to express "deep disappointment" over a U.S. decision earlier this month to back a $13 million World Bank loan to Croatia.
"We believe the arrest and transfer to The Hague of indicted war criminals needs to be treated as a more urgent priority," the senators said in their letter.
"The U.S. should oppose and work against such assistance to Croatia until it apprehends and transfers indicted war criminals who are in territory within its control," the letter said.

It was signed by Democrats Patrick Leahy of Vermont, Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, Dianne Feinstein of California and Barbara Mikulski of Maryland. Republicans were Richard Lugar of Indiana and Alfonse D'Amato of New York.
A World Bank statement on the project said a so-called Investment Recovery Project would strengthen Croatia's banking system and stimulate investment.

It said the Croatian financial sector was still dominated by a small number of "ailing and illiquid" banks and interest rates were high. "The proposed project would attempt to address the weaknesses mentioned above," it said.
The World Bank's board usually meets twice a week, but it was not clear if the loan would be debated at this week's second meeting, due on Wednesday.

The United States has been reviewing international financial assistance to Croatia more rigorously since Albright announced last month that Washington was serious about making aid conditional on compliance with the 1995 Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnia war and on other demands.
